questions.q: What was the immediate trigger for the First Gulf War (1991) and which UN Security Council resolution authorized the use of force against Iraq?
questions.a: The immediate trigger was Iraq's invasion and annexation of Kuwait on August 2, 1990. UN Security Council Resolution 678 (November 29, 1990) authorized member states to use "all necessary means" to uphold Resolution 660 (demanding Iraqi withdrawal) if Iraq did not comply by January 15, 1991. A wrong answer (e.g., citing 9/11 or WMDs) reveals confusion with the 2003 Iraq War or a misunderstanding of the UN's role in collective security.

questions.q: Why did the United States seek UN authorization for the Gulf War instead of acting unilaterally, and what does this reveal about the nature of US hegemony in the early 1990s?
questions.a: The US sought UN authorization to legitimize the intervention, build a broad coalition (including Arab states), and demonstrate that the new world order would operate through collective security mechanisms. This reveals that US hegemony was exercised as "hegemony as structural power" – shaping rules and institutions – rather than purely through unilateral force. A wrong answer suggesting the US didn't need UN approval misses the strategic importance of multilateral legitimacy for sustaining long-term hegemony.

questions.q: Analyze the military-technological innovations showcased during Operation Desert Storm and explain how they demonstrated a "revolution in military affairs" (RMA) that cemented US hard power dominance.
questions.a: Desert Storm showcased precision-guided munitions (PGMs), stealth technology (F-117), GPS navigation, satellite intelligence, and networked command-control systems. These allowed the US to conduct a high-tempo, low-casualty campaign with unprecedented accuracy, rendering traditional massed armor and air defenses obsolete. This technological gap meant no other power could project force similarly, establishing US military hegemony. A wrong answer focusing only on coalition size or leadership misses the transformative technological dimension that defined the "unipolar moment."

questions.q: Compare the international coalition in the 1991 Gulf War with the 2003 Iraq War coalition. What does the difference tell you about the evolution of US hegemony and the role of international legitimacy?
questions.a: The 1991 coalition included 34 nations with explicit UN Security Council authorization (Resolution 678), including key Arab states (Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Syria). The 2003 coalition was smaller ("Coalition of the Willing"), lacked a new UN mandate authorizing force, and faced opposition from traditional allies (France, Germany). This shift shows the erosion of US structural power and the limits of hegemony when legitimacy is perceived as compromised. A wrong answer claiming both coalitions were similar ignores the critical difference in UN authorization and its impact on global perceptions of legitimacy.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument that the First Gulf War was primarily about oil interests rather than collective security. Use evidence from the UN resolutions, coalition composition, and post-war outcomes to support your judgment.
questions.a: While oil was a strategic concern (Kuwait and Saudi oil fields), the war was framed and legitimized through collective security: UN resolutions emphasized sovereignty and territorial integrity (Resolution 660), not resource protection. The coalition included non-oil-dependent nations, and the US did not occupy Kuwait or seize oil assets post-war. The restoration of the Kuwaiti monarchy and the subsequent containment policy (no-fly zones, sanctions) suggest a broader geopolitical strategy. A purely oil-reductionist view fails to explain the multilateral diplomatic effort and the adherence to UN mandates. A wrong answer dismissing collective security as a mere pretext overlooks the institutional constraints that even a hegemon navigates.

questions.q: Create a hypothetical scenario: If a similar invasion occurred today (e.g., a regional power annexing a smaller neighbor), would the UN Security Council likely authorize a comparable coalition? Draft a brief argument considering current great power rivalries (US-China-Russia) and the veto power.
questions.a: A strong answer would note that today's Security Council is more polarized; a veto by a permanent member (likely Russia or China) would block a Resolution 678-style authorization. The 1991 consensus was possible because the USSR was collapsing and China abstained. Today, great power competition makes collective security action harder, illustrating how structural power depends on great power convergence. A poor answer would assume the UN works the same way now, ignoring the shift from unipolarity to multipolarity.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The First Gulf War (1991) was a US-led coalition military operation (Operation Desert Storm) authorized by the UN Security Council to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait, ______ the United States' unprecedented military capability and its ability to shape global security outcomes in the post-Cold War unipolar moment.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are watching a news report from 1991 showing precision-guided missiles hitting targets in Baghdad with ______ accuracy.

Fill in the blank: The First Gulf War (______) was a US-led coalition military operation (Operation Desert Storm) authorized by the UN Security Council to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait, demonstrating the United States' unprecedented military capability and its ability to shape global security outcomes in the post-Cold War unipolar moment.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the First Gulf War showcased US military dominance, the role of UN authorization, the coalition-building process, and the war's significance in establishing the post-Cold War unipolar order, while distinguishing it from the 2003 Iraq War.
